facts.label: Length and weight
facts.value_md: 1 hour, 30% of the course mark. It removes nothing from the final.

facts.label: Covers
facts.value_md: Sessions 1 to 10: starting a project, clean code and tests, the terminal.

facts.label: Format
facts.value_md: Pen and paper, closed book, no devices. Multiple choice with no penalty for a wrong answer, then open questions answered in 5 to 8 lines. You never write code.

facts.label: The sample
facts.value_md: Six multiple choice and three open questions, each open one in three numbered parts. His official answers went on Moodle on 21 October. The real paper keeps the shapes, not the questions or the topics.

facts.label: Not covered
facts.value_md: Git in depth (branching, merging, pull requests) and Docker.

limits_md: The teacher's own words: "You will not write code. Judgement, not memorised flags." You explain, compare, or read a piece of code or tool output and say what it does or what is wrong. His answer sheet adds: "For the open questions, the exam is marked on reasons, not on matching this wording. Different phrasing is fine as long as the idea is there." The sample shows the kind of question and the level of answer, and the exam does not reuse it.

marking.intro_md: His marking guide for the open questions, word for word. Everything in this cram is built on it: an answer scores when it has an idea and a reason, and the reason is tied to the code or the output in front of you.

items.label: Full marks
items.text: the right idea, with a reason (the "because").

items.label: Partial marks
items.text: the right idea with no reason, or a reason that is half right.

items.label: No marks
items.text: an answer that lists terms without connecting them to the code or output.

formula.label: Idea
formula.text_md: Say what is wrong, what changed or which kind it is, in a few words. "Line 15 is a None not handled."

formula.label: Because
formula.text_md: Give the reason: what a teammate cannot do, or what happens when the program runs. This is the mark his guide calls "with a reason". "If the value is None (an empty list or a missing id), the program crashes with an AttributeError for a real user."

formula.label: Point at the code
formula.text_md: Name the line, the identifier or the error you mean: `r[2]`, `line 15`, `[union-attr]`. "The names are bad" scores nothing. "`r[2]` hides which column is the category, so a teammate must guess" scores.

formula.label: Changes, in words
formula.text_md: For "how would you change it", write one sentence per change and the problem it fixes: "I would move the print to the caller, which fixes the two jobs." Never write code.

formula.label: Judgement parts
formula.text_md: "Which is better?" and "Do you accept?" get the verdict first, then the reason, then the real fix. "No. `# type: ignore` hides the warning and the crash stays. Handle the `None`."

formula.label: Length
formula.text_md: One or two sentences per part, 5 to 8 lines for the whole question. Number the parts as the question does and leave none blank.

mcq.text_md: **Answer every one.** A wrong answer costs nothing, so a blank is the only sure zero. If time runs out, put a letter on each question left.
**Read the artefact before the options.** Decide what the error, the output or the diff says, then look for the option that acts on it.

**Cross out the careless moves.** His wrong options are delete `.venv`, reinstall, `--upgrade`, `# type: ignore`, change the type to `Any`, delete the annotations, rerun a flaky test, and trust whichever changed last. Each acts on something the message never mentions, or hides the problem.
**Check the reason as well as the action.** His "why" for each answer is two or three sentences: what the output says, what the right move does, why the others fail.
**For a concept question, apply the course's test.** A refactoring changes structure and keeps behaviour. One function has one job. A failing test shows a mismatch, not a culprit.

plan.text_md: Skim every page. Count the multiple-choice and open questions and note any marks. The paper's mix is not published, so plan by proportion.
Multiple choice, first pass. Artefact first, cross out the careless moves, answer. Dot any you are unsure of and move on.
Open questions, about 8 to 9 minutes each if there are three. Answer every numbered part. If a part is stuck, write the one concrete line you have and move on.
Back to the dotted multiple choice. Re-read the artefact, not your first answer.
A letter on every multiple-choice question and at least one line on every open part. Spread before you polish.

shapes.ask_md: A tool error from `uv`. What should you do next?
Which of these changes is a refactoring?
A `mypy --strict` error on a short snippet. Which fix is most appropriate?
A failing `pytest` line. What can you conclude?
A function that does too much. Which clean-code problem is it?
A pipe such as `grep "food" expenses.csv | wc -l`. What does it print?
Read code and say what is wrong: what it does, two problems, and how you would change it in words.
Compare a diff and two commit messages: what the change does, which message is better, one test in words.
Read `mypy` output: sort the errors into kinds, say which one can crash, and whether you accept `# type: ignore`.
